name: Republic of Lithuania (1918-1940)
info: The independent Lithuanian republic declared on 16 February 1918, governed from Kaunas while Poland held Vilnius, authoritarian under Antanas Smetona from 1926, and occupied and annexed by the Soviet Union in 1940.

facts.capital: Vilnius (claimed); Kaunas, the temporary capital from 1919; Vilnius returned in 1939
facts.founder: The Council of Lithuania (Taryba), led by Jonas Basanavičius

t: The Council of Lithuania adopted the Act of Independence on 16 February 1918, proclaiming an independent republic organised on democratic principles.
For 19 years Kaunas was the temporary capital while Poland held Vilnius, a dispute that dominated Lithuania's politics for the whole interwar period.
The coup of December 1926 installed Antanas Smetona, who ruled as an authoritarian leader until the Soviet ultimatum of June 1940 ended independence.
dyk: To avoid being incorporated into the German Empire, Lithuanians elected the Monaco-born Mindaugas II titular King of Lithuania in July 1918; he never assumed the throne.
ev: On 16 February the Council of Lithuania adopts the Act of Independence of Lithuania
The government moves to Kaunas, and by the end of August the Soviets are pushed out of Lithuanian territory
The Soviet–Lithuanian Peace Treaty is signed, and in October Żeligowski's Mutiny takes Vilnius
Lithuania adopts a final constitution and introduces the litas
The Klaipėda Revolt brings the Klaipėda Region under Lithuania
A military coup installs Antanas Smetona as president
Lithuania cedes the Klaipėda Region to Germany and receives Vilnius under the Soviet–Lithuanian Mutual Assistance Pact
After the Soviet ultimatum of 14 June, Lithuania is annexed as the Lithuanian Soviet Socialist Republic

sections.foundation:
Lithuania had lived under the Russian Empire since the partitions, and a national revival, led by figures such as Jonas Basanavičius and Vincas Kudirka, had grown despite the ban on the Lithuanian press. In 1915 the German Empire occupied the country and incorporated it into Ober Ost. The German occupation government permitted a Vilnius Conference in September 1917, which elected a 20-member Council of Lithuania (Taryba). The Council, led by Basanavičius, declared independence as a German protectorate on 11 December 1917, and on 16 February 1918 adopted the Act of Independence, proclaiming an independent republic organised on democratic principles.

The Germans hindered real independence, and in July 1918 the Council elected Mindaugas II titular king to avoid annexation. After Germany's defeat in November 1918 the Lithuanians formed their first government under Prime Minister Augustinas Voldemaras and adopted a provisional constitution. Soviet forces followed the retreating German army, set up the Lithuanian Soviet Socialist Republic, and took Vilnius on 5 January 1919; the government moved west to Kaunas, the temporary capital.
sections.socioeconomy:
Lithuanian society remained heavily agricultural, with only 20% of the people living in cities. The Constituent Assembly passed a law for land reform, which the Second Seimas continued, introduced a national currency, the litas, and the Second Seimas introduced social support systems and began repaying foreign debt. The first Lithuanian national census took place in 1923. The influence of the Catholic Church was strong and birth rates high: the population rose by 22% to over three million in 1923–1939, despite emigration to South America and elsewhere.

In almost all cities and towns, once dominated by Jews, Poles, Russians and Germans, ethnic Lithuanians became the majority: they were 59% of the residents of Kaunas in 1923, against 7% in 1897. The Klaipėda Region gave the country its only access to the Baltic Sea and was an important industrial centre. When Germany declared an embargo on Lithuanian products after the Neumann–Sass trial of 1934, Lithuania shifted its exports to the United Kingdom, and peasant strikes in Suvalkija were violently suppressed.
sections.military:
The state was won in the Lithuanian Wars of Independence. By mid-January 1919 Soviet forces controlled about two thirds of the country, but the Lithuanian Army under General Silvestras Žukauskas held near Kėdainiai, retook Šiauliai, Radviliškis, Panevėžys and Ukmergė in the spring, and by the end of August had pushed the Soviets out and reached the Daugava. It then defeated the West Russian Volunteer Army, the Bermontians, some 50,000 men armed by Germany, by the end of 1919. A Belarusian unit, the 1st Belarusian Regiment, also served in the Lithuanian Armed Forces.

The Polish–Lithuanian War followed. Polish troops took Vilnius from the Soviets on 21 April 1919, and in August 1919 Józef Piłsudski attempted to overthrow the government in Kaunas. The Suwałki Agreement of 7 October 1920 left Vilnius on the Lithuanian side, but General Lucjan Żeligowski, on Piłsudski's orders, invaded the next day and took the city. The Klaipėda Revolt of January 1923 was the last armed conflict in Lithuania before World War II; in 1938, 1939 and 1940 a weaker Lithuania accepted ultimatums rather than fight.
sections.governance:
The final constitution of August 1922 made Lithuania a democratic state whose Seimas, elected by men and women for three years, chose the president. The First Seimas split 38–38 and was dissolved; the Second, elected in May 1923, was the only one to serve its full term. The country was divided into 23 counties, with a further 11, Vilnius among them, allocated to the territory occupied by Poland. A Ministry for Belarusian Affairs functioned in 1918–1924.

In May 1926 the bloc led by the Lithuanian Christian Democratic Party lost its majority, and in December a military coup, supported by the Lithuanian Nationalists Union and the Christian Democrats, installed Antanas Smetona as president and Voldemaras as prime minister. Smetona suppressed the opposition, dissolved the Seimas in May 1927 and in 1928 announced a fifth provisional constitution that vastly increased the president's powers. He took the title "tautos vadas" (leader of the nation) and began building a cult of personality. The Fourth Seimas of 1936, with all parties but the National Union eliminated, adopted in February 1938 a constitution granting him still greater powers.
sections.impact:
The interwar years gave birth to the development of Lithuanian press, literature, music, arts and theatre, and to a comprehensive system of education with Lithuanian as the language of instruction; primary and secondary schools were expanded and institutions of higher learning established in Kaunas. Lithuania gained international recognition and membership of the League of Nations. In the Soviet–Lithuanian Peace Treaty of 12 July 1920 the Soviet Union recognised a fully independent Lithuania and its claims to the Vilnius Region.

The Vilnius dispute shaped its foreign relations. The League of Nations tried to mediate, and Paul Hymans proposed plans for a Polish–Lithuanian union, but the Conference of Ambassadors awarded Vilnius to Poland in March 1923 and Lithuania broke off all relations; the two countries remained officially at war over the city until Lithuania accepted the 1938 Polish ultimatum. The capture of the Klaipėda Region, detached from East Prussia, during the Ruhr Crisis of 1923, and its autonomy within Lithuania from May 1924, set it against Germany, whose inhabitants of the region resisted Lithuanian rule in the 1930s.
sections.decline:
On 20 March 1939 Germany's ultimatum forced the cession of the Klaipėda Region, a major blow to the economy that obliged Smetona to bring the opposition into government. The Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact first assigned Lithuania to Germany, but after Smetona refused to join the invasion of Poland it passed to the Soviet sphere. Under the Soviet–Lithuanian Mutual Assistance Pact of 10 October 1939 the Soviet Union transferred Vilnius to Lithuania in exchange for stationing 20,000 Soviet troops in the country, a virtual sacrifice of independence: "Vilnius is ours, but Lithuania is Russia's".

On 14 June 1940 the Soviet ultimatum demanded a pro-Soviet government and more Red Army troops. Lithuania accepted, Smetona fled as 150,000 Soviet troops crossed the border, and Vladimir Dekanozov formed a puppet People's Government under Justas Paleckis and organised show elections. On 21 July the People's Seimas voted to make Lithuania the Lithuanian Soviet Socialist Republic, and the Supreme Soviet approved its annexation on 3 August 1940. Sovietization, nationalisation and arrests followed, and in June 1941 some 12,600 people were deported to the Gulag.

summary: Interwar Lithuania was a small agricultural republic declared in 1918 and defended in the Wars of Independence, which built a Lithuanian-language culture and schools from its temporary capital, Kaunas, while Poland held Vilnius. Democratic until the coup of 1926 and then ruled by Antanas Smetona, it was occupied and annexed by the Soviet Union in 1940.

Snyder, Timothy, The Reconstruction of Nations: Poland, Ukraine, Lithuania, Belarus, 1569-1999 (Yale University Press, 2003)
Lukowski, Jerzy; Zawadzki, Hubert, A Concise History of Poland (Cambridge University Press, 2001)
Butterwick, Richard, Lithuania: A History (Oxford University Press, 2025)

pointDescs.1918: The Council of Lithuania adopts the Act of Independence, though German troops remain in the country.
pointDescs.1919: The government moves to Kaunas; by the end of August the army has pushed the Soviets out.
pointDescs.1920: The Soviet Union recognises Lithuania, but Żeligowski's Mutiny takes Vilnius in October.
pointDescs.1922: A final constitution, land reform, the litas and membership of the League of Nations.
pointDescs.1923: The Klaipėda Revolt gives Lithuania the Klaipėda Region and its only access to the sea.
pointDescs.1926: A military coup installs Antanas Smetona, who suppresses the opposition.
pointDescs.1934: Nazi activists in Klaipėda are tried; Germany answers with an embargo and exports shift to Britain.
pointDescs.1938: Lithuania accepts the Polish ultimatum and restores relations with Poland.
pointDescs.1939: Germany takes the Klaipėda Region; the Soviet Union hands over Vilnius in exchange for 20,000 troops.
pointDescs.1940: The Soviet ultimatum of 14 June leads to occupation and annexation as the Lithuanian SSR.

notes: The saved article is the general 'History of Lithuania', not an article on the interwar state; I used only its 1918-1940 section and the parts around it, so detail is thinner than a dedicated article would give. The Klaipeda figures: the article says 'various sources' give 41.9% German, 27.1% Memellandisch, 26.6% Lithuanian; I left them out. Butterwick (2025) is in the article's Further reading but covers all of Lithuanian history; the editor may drop it.
